resolutions.rationale: Nørmark fairly stresses testing and correction, but his dream-medicine comparison and description of religion as insane do not engage Turek’s offered historical and scientific evidence charitably.

The evolutionary account explains how cooperative dispositions can arise, but Turek’s live challenge concerned what makes moral claims objectively true, so the ontology question remains largely unanswered.
Nørmark openly states his preference for a godless world, yet calling nonbelief the adult position and comparing believers with children materially weakens charity beyond the argument supplied.
Costly commitment bears against deliberate fabrication, but sincerity alone cannot distinguish accurate miracle testimony from mistake, legendary development, or inherited tradition.
The asserted deaths of eleven disciples and their opportunities to recant are essential premises but receive no disciple-specific support in the exchange, while the UFO contrast remains anecdotal.
Turek directly contests Nørmark’s suggestion of deliberate invention, but the reply does not address the separate live alternatives of perceptual error and later story development.
The move helps the historical route by narrowing deliberate fraud, while its conclusion remains limited because sincere costly belief does not independently establish resurrection.
The fabrication-versus-cost inference is easy to reconstruct, but the crucial claims that disciples died for the belief and could have saved themselves are left materially undefined.
Turek fairly targets fabrication, yet saying invention requires more faith overstates what costly belief shows and gives insufficient consideration to sincere error.
The genetic-origin distinction addresses a naturalistic psychology line, but Nørmark later explicitly frames brain origin as comparative probability rather than entailment, limiting the reply’s fit.
The move materially protects the reason route by separating causal origin from truth, although it does not itself establish the cosmological, moral, or historical evidence Turek invokes.
Turek clearly separates why a belief is held from whether it is true and redirects evaluation to evidence; the central inference remains recoverable despite caption noise.
The general origin-versus-truth principle is fair, but calling Nørmark’s position a genetic fallacy before engaging his expressly probabilistic clarification weakens charity.
The survival-to-determinism-to-reaction-and-self-defeat chain is explicit and auditable, despite loose shifts among atheism, naturalism, materialism, evolution, and determinism.
The move directly answers categorical-sounding miracle skepticism by demanding evidence for each case, but Nørmark later clarifies that he never categorically ruled miracles out.
Nørmark conflates applying a premise to things that begin with placing God under natural laws; his conclusion that natural laws precede God does not follow from Turek’s stated exemption.
The objection targets the creator bridge directly, but it neither supplies an alternative account nor defeats Turek’s restricted premise that only things with beginnings require originating causes.
Although Nørmark admits he is not a physicist, he moves from an underdeveloped causal objection to calling it an indication that God never existed, exceeding the analysis presented.
The child and pain examples explain moral recognition and practical conduct, but Turek had expressly separated those questions from the objective ground of moral truth.
The audio verification confirms Nørmark’s ownership of the history-and-myth account and its qualification, while uncertain names are excluded from the assessment rather than treated as defects.
Turek answers the moderator’s violence challenge by separating doctrine from misuse, but he does not engage Nørmark’s stronger concern about higher ideological ends overriding persons.
The doctrine-versus-abuse distinction bears on the moral route, while the unsupported Hitler extension relies on association and adds little motion-level support.
Nørmark consistently makes the limited logical point that lacking a mechanism does not license inserting God, without pretending that his uncertainty itself supplies a positive cosmology.
Nørmark candidly offers no cosmological mechanism and appeals generally to scientific expertise without identifying its evidence, so the positive naturalistic support is thin.
He directly answers Turek’s demand for a better explanation by explaining why a critic may withhold a mechanism without thereby granting the proposed divine cause.
The reply strongly serves Nørmark’s qualified critical burden by blocking an inference from cosmological ignorance to God, without assuming a universal-disproof obligation.
His admission of uncertainty and core ignorance-versus-magic distinction are clear, but the baking and engine analogies and attention-seeking aside reduce precision.
Nørmark expressly disclaims expertise and certainty, which properly calibrates the limited conclusion, though his remark about dissenting scientists seeking attention is uncharitable.
Dependence of consciousness on brain states supports a physical basis, but moving from modifiability to identity and then to the nonexistence of a soul is not deductively sufficient.
The ability to alter or eliminate consciousness through physical intervention is relevant empirical support, though Nørmark provides no specific studies or cases in the debate.
This is a constructive natural account of mind rather than a reply to an earlier selected pro move, and it appropriately develops Nørmark’s own subsidiary mind burden.
The brain-dependence evidence materially advances the naturalistic mind route, but it does not exclude nonreductive or dualist accounts that also permit such dependence.
Nørmark reasonably cites physical dependence of mental capacities, but his categorical statement that there is no soul is more confident than the presented evidence establishes.
The closing repeats cosmology, morality, disciple contact, martyrdom, and influence without adding checks on the contested historical and inferential premises supporting those claims.
The four-part cumulative case and final conclusion are readily identifiable, although the extended redemption and influence passages blur argument, exhortation, and historical inference.
Nørmark preserves the value of love despite its physical basis, but calling God a creature in the sky and ending with an absolute cheated framing caricatures the opposing view.
No separate debate-wide adjustment is warranted because Turek’s creator, morality, history, reason, and closing burdens are already represented in the locked move ratings.
No separate debate-wide adjustment is warranted because Nørmark’s qualified probability burden and positive naturalistic routes are already represented in the locked move ratings.
